topic: Instructor responsibilities and flight instruction techniques

notes.front: What is the Aviator’s Model Code of Conduct?
notes.back: Broad guidance and recommendations for general aviation pilots to improve airmanship and flight safety, and to sustain and improve the general aviation community.
notes.explanation: The handbook describes it as a vision of excellence in general aviation.
notes.source: Aviation Instructor's Handbook (FAA-H-8083-9B), ch. 8, “Aviator's Model Code of Conduct”, p. 8-6
notes.evidence: The Aviator’s Model Code of Conduct presents broad guidance and recommendations for General Aviation (GA) pilots to improve airmanship, flight safety, and to sustain and improve the GA community. The Code of Conduct presents a vision of excellence in GA aviation.
notes.example: Like a professional body’s code of good practice that its members choose to adopt as their own.

notes.front: What is the FAA Safety Team (FAASTeam)?
notes.back: An FAA team dedicated to improving the aviation safety record by conveying safety principles and practices through training, outreach and education.
notes.explanation: The handbook offers partnering with the FAASTeam as a way for an instructor to advocate safety.
notes.source: Aviation Instructor's Handbook (FAA-H-8083-9B), ch. 8, “Safety Practices and Accident Prevention”, p. 8-7
notes.evidence: Another way for the instructor to advocate safety is to partner with the FAA Safety Team (FAASTeam). The FAASTeam is dedicated to improving the aviation safety record by conveying safety principles and practices through training, outreach, and education.
notes.example: Like a local road-safety partnership that runs free evening talks for drivers, but for pilots and instructors.

notes.front: What is the telling-and-doing technique?
notes.back: A technique of flight instruction that applies the demonstration-performance method in three steps, with specific variations for flight instruction.
notes.explanation: It borrows the structure of the demonstration-performance method and adapts it to teaching in the aircraft.
notes.source: Aviation Instructor's Handbook (FAA-H-8083-9B), ch. 9, “The Telling-and-Doing Technique”, p. 9-6
notes.evidence: The demonstration-performance method can be applied to the telling-and-doing technique of flight instruction in three steps. However, the telling-and-doing technique includes specific variations for flight instruction.
notes.example: Like teaching someone to reverse a trailer: you talk it through as you do it, then they talk you through it, then they talk themselves through it.

notes.front: What is the positive exchange of flight controls?
notes.back: A strongly recommended three-step procedure for handing control between pilots, so that learner and instructor always clearly understand who has control.
notes.explanation: The handbook calls the three-step process a proven procedure.
notes.source: Aviation Instructor's Handbook (FAA-H-8083-9B), ch. 9, “Positive Exchange of Flight Controls”, p. 9-8
notes.evidence: During flight training, there should always be a clear understanding between learners and flight instructors about who has control of the aircraft. The preflight briefing should include procedures for the exchange of flight controls. A positive three-step process in the exchange of flight controls between pilots is a proven procedure and one that is strongly recommended.
notes.example: Like a relay handover in which the runner does not let go of the baton until the next runner has a firm grip on it.

notes.front: What is the sterile flight deck rule?
notes.back: Section 121.542, which requires airline flight crewmembers to refrain from nonessential activities during critical phases of flight.
notes.explanation: The rule is commonly known by this name rather than by its section number.
notes.source: Aviation Instructor's Handbook (FAA-H-8083-9B), ch. 9, “Sterile Flight Deck Rule”, p. 9-9
notes.evidence: Commonly known as the "sterile flight deck rule," Title 14 of the Code of Federal Regulations (14 CFR) part 121, section 121.542 requires airline flight crewmembers to refrain from nonessential activities during critical phases of flight.
notes.example: Like a surgical team that stops all small talk during the delicate part of an operation.

notes.front: What is integrated flight instruction?
notes.back: Flight instruction in which learners are taught to perform manoeuvres both by outside visual references and by reference to flight instruments.
notes.explanation: Both kinds of reference are taught for the same manoeuvres.
notes.source: Aviation Instructor's Handbook (FAA-H-8083-9B), ch. 9, “Integrated Flight Instruction”, p. 9-10
notes.evidence: Integrated flight instruction is flight instruction during which learners are taught to perform flight maneuvers both by outside visual references and by reference to flight instruments.
notes.example: Like a new driver learning to glance at the speedometer from the very first lesson instead of judging speed only by eye.

notes.front: Under “helping learners”, does making each lesson a pleasurable experience mean making things easy?
notes.back: No: the instructor does not sacrifice standards of performance to make things easy.
notes.explanation: A pleasurable lesson helps the learner keep a high level of motivation, but the standards stay.
notes.source: Aviation Instructor's Handbook (FAA-H-8083-9B), ch. 8, “Helping Learners”, p. 8-1
notes.evidence: By making each lesson a pleasurable experience, the instructor helps the learner maintain a high level of motivation. This does not mean the instructor sacrifices standards of performance to make things easy.

notes.front: To tailor teaching technique to a learner, what does the flight instructor analyse?
notes.back: The learner’s personality, thinking and ability.
notes.explanation: No two learners are alike, so a method that works for one may not work equally well for another.
notes.source: Aviation Instructor's Handbook (FAA-H-8083-9B), ch. 8, “Providing Adequate Instruction”, p. 8-1
notes.evidence: To tailor his or her teaching technique to the learner, the flight instructor analyzes the learner’s personality, thinking, and ability. No two learners are alike, and a particular method of instruction may not be equally effective for all learners.

notes.front: Is the Airman Certification Standards book a teaching document or a testing document?
notes.back: A testing document, not a teaching document.
notes.explanation: The instructor trains the applicant to its standards in every task, but it is not the teaching plan.
notes.source: Aviation Instructor's Handbook (FAA-H-8083-9B), ch. 8, “Standards of Performance”, p. 8-2
notes.evidence: An aviation instructor is responsible for training an applicant to established standards in all subject matter areas, procedures, and maneuvers included in the tasks within each area of operation in the appropriate Airman Certification (ACS)/Airman Practical Test Standards (PTS). It should be emphasized that the ACS/PTS book is a testing document, not a teaching document.

notes.front: The handbook sums up: emphasize the positive because {{c1::positive instruction results in positive learning}}.
notes.back: positive instruction results in positive learning
notes.explanation: It adds that a learner’s failure to perform often results from the instructor’s inability to transfer the required information.
notes.source: Aviation Instructor's Handbook (FAA-H-8083-9B), ch. 8, “Emphasizing the Positive”, p. 8-3
notes.evidence: In essence, a learner’s failure to perform often results from an instructor’s inability to transfer the required information. Emphasize the positive because positive instruction results in positive learning.

notes.front: Which rule for minimising learner frustration rests on the idea that more can be gained from wanting to learn than from being forced to learn?
notes.back: Motivate learners.
notes.explanation: When learners see the benefits and purpose of a lesson or course, their enjoyment and effort increase.
notes.source: Aviation Instructor's Handbook (FAA-H-8083-9B), ch. 8, “Minimizing Learner Frustration”, p. 8-4
notes.evidence: Motivate learners—more can be gained from wanting to learn than from being forced to learn. Too often, learners do not realize how a particular lesson or course can help them reach an important goal. When learners can see the benefits and purpose of the lesson or course, their enjoyment and their efforts increase.

notes.front: Which rule for minimising learner frustration answers the insecurity learners feel when they do not know what is expected of them?
notes.back: Keep learners informed.
notes.explanation: Telling learners what is expected of them, and what they can expect in return, reduces that insecurity.
notes.source: Aviation Instructor's Handbook (FAA-H-8083-9B), ch. 8, “Minimizing Learner Frustration”, p. 8-4
notes.evidence: Keep learners informed—learners feel insecure when they do not know what is expected of them or what is going to happen to them. Instructors can minimize feelings of insecurity by telling learners what is expected of them and what they can expect in return.

notes.front: Which rule for minimising learner frustration warns that thinking only of the whole group aims at an average personality that fits no one?
notes.back: Approach learners as individuals.
notes.explanation: Efforts aimed at the whole group end up aimed at an average that fits no one.
notes.source: Aviation Instructor's Handbook (FAA-H-8083-9B), ch. 8, “Minimizing Learner Frustration”, p. 8-4
notes.evidence: Approach learners as individuals—when instructors limit their thinking to the whole group without considering the individuals who make up that group, their efforts are directed at an average personality that really fits no one.

notes.front: Which rule for minimising learner frustration warns that praise given too freely becomes valueless?
notes.back: Give credit when due.
notes.explanation: Deserved praise pays dividends in learner effort and achievement.
notes.source: Aviation Instructor's Handbook (FAA-H-8083-9B), ch. 8, “Minimizing Learner Frustration”, p. 8-4
notes.evidence: Praise pays dividends in learner effort and achievement when deserved, but when given too freely, it becomes valueless.

notes.front: Which rule for minimising learner frustration says errors must be identified and explained, or they will probably be perpetuated through faulty practice?
notes.back: Criticize constructively.
notes.explanation: Telling a learner the work is unsatisfactory with no explanation leads to frustration.
notes.source: Aviation Instructor's Handbook (FAA-H-8083-9B), ch. 8, “Minimizing Learner Frustration”, p. 8-4
notes.evidence: If a learner has made an earnest effort but is told that the work is unsatisfactory, with no other explanation, frustration occurs. Errors cannot be corrected if they are not identified, and if they are not identified, they will probably be perpetuated through faulty practice.

notes.front: What does the handbook call the flight instructor’s job?
notes.back: To “mold” the learner pilot into a safe pilot who takes a professional approach to flying.
notes.explanation: Other flight instructor responsibilities are set out in part 61 of the regulations and in advisory circulars.
notes.source: Aviation Instructor's Handbook (FAA-H-8083-9B), ch. 8, “Flight Instructor Responsibilities”, p. 8-5
notes.evidence: The flight instructor’s job is to "mold" the learner pilot into a safe pilot who takes a professional approach to flying. Other flight instructor responsibilities can be found in Title 14 of the Code of Federal Regulations (14 CFR) part 61 and FAA advisory circulars (ACs).

notes.front: What additional responsibility may flight instructors have, compared with other aviation instructors?
notes.back: Evaluating learner pilots and deciding when they are ready to solo.
notes.explanation: All aviation instructors carry a heavy responsibility because their learners will fly, service or repair aircraft.
notes.source: Aviation Instructor's Handbook (FAA-H-8083-9B), ch. 8, “Flight Instructor Responsibilities”, p. 8-5
notes.evidence: All aviation instructors shoulder an enormous responsibility because their learners will ultimately be flying, servicing, or repairing aircraft. Flight instructors may have the additional responsibility regarding evaluation of learner pilots and deciding when they are ready to solo.

notes.front: What are two of the common special emphasis items the handbook lists?
notes.back: Positive aircraft control; stall and spin awareness; collision avoidance (among others).
notes.explanation: The list also includes procedures for positive exchange of flight controls.
notes.source: Aviation Instructor's Handbook (FAA-H-8083-9B), ch. 8, “Flight Instructor Responsibilities”, p. 8-6
notes.evidence: PTS lists special emphasis items. Some common items include: 1. Positive aircraft control 2. Procedures for positive exchange of flight controls 3. Stall and spin awareness 4. Collision avoidance

notes.front: Why should an instructor not ignore a learner’s discomfort from unfamiliar noises, G-force or an uneasy stomach?
notes.back: A sick learner is preoccupied and may not have the mental or physical capacity to learn.
notes.explanation: The handbook adds that these sensations can usually be overcome by understanding their causes.
notes.source: Aviation Instructor's Handbook (FAA-H-8083-9B), ch. 8, “Physiological Obstacles for Flight Learners”, p. 8-5
notes.evidence: These negative sensations can usually be overcome by understanding the nature of their causes. Remember, a sick learner is preoccupied and may not have the mental or physical capacity to learn.

notes.front: In the instructor’s code of ethics, what should the pilot or technician make the number one priority?
notes.back: Safety.
notes.explanation: The code describes a good aviation citizen, and safety heads its list.
notes.source: Aviation Instructor's Handbook (FAA-H-8083-9B), ch. 5, “Instructor's Code of Ethics”, p. 5-3
notes.evidence: The following code describes the concept of a good aviation citizen. An aviation instructor needs to remember he or she is teaching a pilot or technician who should: 1. Make safety the number one priority,

notes.front: Under the instructor’s code of ethics, what should the pilot develop and exercise in making decisions?
notes.back: Good judgement.
notes.explanation: It is the second quality in the code’s picture of a good aviation citizen.
notes.source: Aviation Instructor's Handbook (FAA-H-8083-9B), ch. 5, “Instructor's Code of Ethics”, p. 5-3
notes.evidence: 2. Develop and exercise good judgment in making decisions,

notes.front: Under the instructor’s code of ethics, what should the pilot do about risk?
notes.back: Recognise and manage it effectively.
notes.explanation: It is the third quality in the code’s picture of a good aviation citizen.
notes.source: Aviation Instructor's Handbook (FAA-H-8083-9B), ch. 5, “Instructor's Code of Ethics”, p. 5-3
notes.evidence: 3. Recognize and manage risk effectively,

notes.front: The instructor’s code of ethics describes a pilot who should be {{c1::accountable}} for his or her actions.
notes.back: accountable
notes.explanation: It is the fourth quality in the code’s picture of a good aviation citizen.
notes.source: Aviation Instructor's Handbook (FAA-H-8083-9B), ch. 5, “Instructor's Code of Ethics”, p. 5-3
notes.evidence: 4. Be accountable for his or her actions,

notes.front: Under the instructor’s code of ethics, with which two qualities should the pilot act?
notes.back: Responsibility and courtesy.
notes.explanation: It is the fifth quality in the code’s picture of a good aviation citizen.
notes.source: Aviation Instructor's Handbook (FAA-H-8083-9B), ch. 5, “Instructor's Code of Ethics”, p. 5-3
notes.evidence: 5. Act with responsibility and courtesy,

notes.front: What is the last item in the instructor’s code of ethics for a good aviation citizen?
notes.back: Adhere to applicable laws and regulations.
notes.explanation: It follows the item on prudent operating practices and personal operating parameters.
notes.source: Aviation Instructor's Handbook (FAA-H-8083-9B), ch. 5, “Instructor's Code of Ethics”, p. 5-3
notes.evidence: 6. Adhere to prudent operating practices and personal operating parameters, and 7. Adhere to applicable laws and regulations.

notes.front: How many sections does the Aviator’s Model Code of Conduct have? Name two.
notes.back: Seven; for example Security and Use of Technology.
notes.explanation: The sections run from general responsibilities of aviators to the advancement and promotion of general aviation.
notes.source: Aviation Instructor's Handbook (FAA-H-8083-9B), ch. 8, “Aviator's Model Code of Conduct”, p. 8-6
notes.evidence: The code of conduct consists of the following seven sections: 1. General Responsibilities of Aviators 2. Passengers and People on the Surface 3. Training and Proficiency 4. Security 5. Environmental Issues 6. Use of Technology 7. Advancement and Promotion of General Aviation

notes.front: Why may even the strictest compliance with regulations not guarantee safety?
notes.back: Rules address known or suspected conditions, and a new combination of circumstances they did not contemplate can always arise.
notes.explanation: The handbook asks instructors to be proactive about the safety of training activities.
notes.source: Aviation Instructor's Handbook (FAA-H-8083-9B), ch. 8, “Safety Practices and Accident Prevention”, p. 8-6
notes.evidence: Rules and regulations are designed to address known or suspected conditions detrimental to safety, but there is always a chance that some new combination of circumstances not contemplated by the regulations will arise. It is important for aviation instructors to be proactive to ensure the safety of flight or maintenance training activities.

notes.front: Which professional quality is lost when an instructor tries to hide inadequacy behind a smokescreen of unrelated instruction?
notes.back: Sincerity.
notes.explanation: Hiding inadequacy that way makes it impossible to command the learner’s respect and full attention.
notes.source: Aviation Instructor's Handbook (FAA-H-8083-9B), ch. 8, “Sincerity”, p. 8-8
notes.evidence: However, the aviation instructor should be straightforward and honest at all times. Attempting to hide inadequacy behind a smokescreen of unrelated instruction makes it impossible for the instructor to command the respect and full attention of a learner.

notes.front: Under “acceptance of the learner”, how should the instructor accept learners?
notes.back: As they are, including all their faults and problems.
notes.explanation: Acceptance extends to all of the learner’s faults and problems.
notes.source: Aviation Instructor's Handbook (FAA-H-8083-9B), ch. 8, “Acceptance of the Learner”, p. 8-8
notes.evidence: The instructor needs to accept learners as they are, including all their faults and problems.

notes.front: Which personal habit does the handbook call perhaps the most important to an instructor’s professional image?
notes.back: The exercise of common courtesy.
notes.explanation: A rude, thoughtless, inattentive instructor cannot hold a learner’s respect, however able a pilot.
notes.source: Aviation Instructor's Handbook (FAA-H-8083-9B), ch. 8, “Personal Appearance and Habits”, p. 8-9
notes.evidence: The exercise of common courtesy is perhaps the most important of these. An instructor who is rude, thoughtless, and inattentive cannot hold the respect of a learner, regardless of the instructor’s ability as a pilot or aviation maintenance technician.

notes.front: What does an instructor’s use of profanity and obscene language lead to?
notes.back: Distrust or, at best, a lack of complete confidence in the instructor.
notes.explanation: The professional instructor speaks positively and descriptively, without profanity.
notes.source: Aviation Instructor's Handbook (FAA-H-8083-9B), ch. 8, “Proper Language”, p. 8-9
notes.evidence: the use of profanity and obscene language leads to distrust or, at best, to a lack of complete confidence in the instructor. Many people object to such language. The professional instructor speaks normally, without inhibitions, and speaks positively and descriptively, without profanity.

notes.front: When evaluating demonstrated ability, what does the instructor consider rather than merely the overall performance?
notes.back: The learner’s mastery of the elements involved in the manoeuvre or procedure.
notes.explanation: The standards used are the established ones, suitably modified for the learner’s experience and stage of development.
notes.source: Aviation Instructor's Handbook (FAA-H-8083-9B), ch. 8, “Demonstrated Ability”, p. 8-10
notes.evidence: Evaluation of demonstrated ability during flight or maintenance instruction is based upon established standards of performance, suitably modified to apply to the learner’s experience and stage of development as a pilot or mechanic. The evaluation considers the learner’s mastery of the elements involved in the maneuver or procedure, rather than merely the overall performance.

notes.front: How do successful, professional aviation instructors regard their own qualifications and abilities?
notes.back: They do not become complacent or satisfied, and stay alert for ways to improve.
notes.explanation: They stay alert to improve their qualifications, effectiveness and service to learners.
notes.source: Aviation Instructor's Handbook (FAA-H-8083-9B), ch. 8, “Professional Development”, p. 8-10
notes.evidence: Successful, professional aviation instructors do not become complacent or satisfied with their own qualifications and abilities and are constantly alert for ways to improve their qualifications, effectiveness, and the services they provide to learners.

notes.front: Into which three categories does the FAA separate flight simulation trainers?
notes.back: Full flight simulator, flight training device and aviation training device.
notes.explanation: The handbook lists these three under the use of flight simulation training devices.
notes.source: Aviation Instructor's Handbook (FAA-H-8083-9B), ch. 9, “Use of Flight Simulation Training Devices”, p. 9-2
notes.evidence: The FAA separates flight simulation trainers into three specific categories: ⦁ Full Flight Simulator (FFS) ⦁ Flight Training Device (FTD) ⦁ Aviation Training Device (ATD)

notes.front: What are the three steps of the telling-and-doing technique, in order?
notes.back: Instructor tells, instructor does; learner tells, instructor does; learner tells, learner does.
notes.explanation: The glossary adds a last stage in which the instructor evaluates while the learner performs.
notes.source: Aviation Instructor's Handbook (FAA-H-8083-9B), glossary, “Glossary: Telling-and-doing technique”, p. G-7
notes.evidence: A technique of flight instruction that consists of the instructor first telling the learner about a new procedure and then demonstrating it. This is followed by the learner telling and the instructor doing. Third, the learner explains the new procedure while doing it. Last, the instructor evaluates while the learner performs the procedure.

image.alt: Flow of four boxes: Step 1, instructor tells, instructor does; Step 2, learner tells, instructor does; Step 3, learner tells, learner does; then last, instructor evaluates.
image.credit: Drawn for this deck from the Aviation Instructor's Handbook (FAA-H-8083-9B), p. 9-7 to 9-8 and the glossary entry for the telling-and-doing technique

notes.front: In which step of the telling-and-doing technique is the learner passive, and how should the demonstration relate to the explanation?
notes.back: Instructor tells, instructor does; the demonstration should match the explanation as closely as possible, in the same sequence.
notes.explanation: Following the same sequence avoids confusion and gives reinforcement.
notes.source: Aviation Instructor's Handbook (FAA-H-8083-9B), ch. 9, “Instructor Tells—Instructor Does”, p. 9-7
notes.evidence: This is the only step in which the learner plays a passive role. It is important for the demonstration to conform to the explanation as closely as possible. In addition, it should be demonstrated in the same sequence in which it was explained so as to avoid confusion and provide reinforcement.

notes.front: In the “learner tells, instructor does” step, what does the learner gain by not flying?
notes.back: Freed from performing the manoeuvre and from worry about its outcome, the learner can organise thoughts on the steps and techniques.
notes.explanation: In the handbook’s words, this is one of two benefits of the step.
notes.source: Aviation Instructor's Handbook (FAA-H-8083-9B), ch. 9, “Learner Tells—Instructor Does”, p. 9-8
notes.evidence: Two benefits accrue from this step: the learner, being freed from the need to concentrate on performance of the maneuver and from concern about its outcome, is able to organize his or her thoughts regarding the steps involved and the techniques to be used.

notes.front: In the telling-and-doing technique, in which step does learning take place and are performance habits formed?
notes.back: The third step, learner tells, learner does (application).
notes.explanation: Meaningful learning happens here if the learner was prepared and the procedure fully explained and demonstrated.
notes.source: Aviation Instructor's Handbook (FAA-H-8083-9B), ch. 9, “Learner Tells—Learner Does”, p. 9-8
notes.evidence: Application is the third step in this method. This is where learning takes place and where performance habits are formed. If the learner has been adequately prepared and the procedure or maneuver fully explained and demonstrated, meaningful learning occurs.

notes.front: What are the three steps of the positive exchange of flight controls?
notes.back: “You have the flight controls.” “I have the flight controls.” “You have the flight controls,” with a visual check.
notes.explanation: The first pilot repeats the handover and visually confirms it, so there is no doubt who is flying.
notes.source: Flight Instructor for Airplane Category ACS (FAA-S-ACS-25), Appendix, “Positive Exchange of Flight Controls”, p. 107
notes.evidence: When one pilot seeks to have the other pilot take control of the aircraft, they will say, "You have the flight controls." • The second pilot acknowledges immediately by saying, "I have the flight controls." • The first pilot again says, "You have the flight controls," and visually confirms the exchange.

image.alt: Three stacked boxes: 1, the pilot handing over says “You have the flight controls”; 2, the pilot taking over says at once “I have the flight controls”; 3, the pilot handing over says again “You have the flight controls”, then makes a visual check.
image.credit: Drawn for this deck from the Flight Instructor for Airplane Category ACS (FAA-S-ACS-25), “Positive Exchange of Flight Controls”

notes.front: What problem led the handbook to stress the positive exchange of flight controls?
notes.back: Numerous accidents from a lack of communication or misunderstanding over who had actual control, particularly between learners and flight instructors.
notes.explanation: Setting the procedure during initial training is meant to form a habit that lasts a flying career.
notes.source: Aviation Instructor's Handbook (FAA-H-8083-9B), ch. 9, “Positive Exchange of Flight Controls”, p. 9-8
notes.evidence: Numerous accidents have occurred due to a lack of communication or misunderstanding regarding who had actual control of the aircraft, particularly between learners and flight instructors. Establishing the following procedure during initial training will ensure the formation of a habit pattern that should stay with learners throughout their flying careers.

notes.front: When a flight instructor must take control, what should the instructor do and say, and why not leave the learner on the controls?
notes.back: Take the controls and calmly announce “I have the flight controls”; with the learner on the controls, the instructor may lack full control.
notes.explanation: Anxious learners can be very strong and often react inappropriately to the situation.
notes.source: Aviation Instructor's Handbook (FAA-H-8083-9B), ch. 9, “Positive Exchange of Flight Controls”, p. 9-9
notes.evidence: When necessary, the instructor should take the controls and calmly announce, "I have the flight controls." If an instructor allows a learner to remain on the controls, the instructor may not have full and effective control of the aircraft. Anxious learners can be incredibly strong and usually exhibit reactions inappropriate to the situation.

notes.front: Under the sterile flight deck rule, what are the critical phases of flight?
notes.back: All ground operations involving taxi, takeoff and landing, and all other operations below 10,000 feet except cruise flight.
notes.explanation: Nonessential activities include eating, reading a newspaper or chatting.
notes.source: Aviation Instructor's Handbook (FAA-H-8083-9B), ch. 9, “Sterile Flight Deck Rule”, p. 9-9
notes.evidence: As defined in the regulation, critical phases of flight are all ground operations involving taxi, takeoff, and landing, and all other flight operations below 10,000 feet except cruise flight. Nonessential activities include such activities as eating, reading a newspaper, or chatting.

notes.front: The intentional practice of stalls and spins seldom resulted in an accident; the real danger was {{c1::inadvertent stalls induced by distractions}} during routine flight.
notes.back: inadvertent stalls induced by distractions
notes.explanation: Deliberate stall and spin practice was not the main hazard.
notes.source: Aviation Instructor's Handbook (FAA-H-8083-9B), ch. 9, “Use of Distractions”, p. 9-9
notes.evidence: The intentional practice of stalls and spins seldom resulted in an accident. The real danger was inadvertent stalls induced by distractions during routine flight situations.

notes.front: What is the purpose of the FAA’s policy of using certain distractions on practical tests?
notes.back: To determine that applicants can cope with distractions while keeping the aircraft control needed for safe flight.
notes.explanation: The distractions test coping while keeping the aircraft under control.
notes.source: Aviation Instructor's Handbook (FAA-H-8083-9B), ch. 9, “Use of Distractions”, p. 9-10
notes.evidence: The FAA has established a policy for use of certain distractions on practical tests for pilot certification. The purpose is to determine that applicants possess the skills required to cope with distractions while maintaining the degree of aircraft control required for safe flight.

notes.front: In integrated flight instruction, no distinction in the pilot’s {{c1::operation of the flight controls}} is permitted, whether outside references or instruments are used.
notes.back: operation of the flight controls
notes.explanation: The same control handling applies whichever references the pilot is using.
notes.source: Aviation Instructor's Handbook (FAA-H-8083-9B), ch. 9, “Integrated Flight Instruction”, p. 9-10
notes.evidence: No distinction in the pilot’s operation of the flight controls is permitted, regardless of whether outside references or instrument indications are used for the performance of the maneuver.

notes.front: What must the instructor make sure learners understand about the instrument work in integrated flight instruction?
notes.back: It does not prepare them for operations in marginal weather or instrument meteorological conditions.
notes.explanation: An introduction to the instruments is not preparation for flight in those conditions.
notes.source: Aviation Instructor's Handbook (FAA-H-8083-9B), ch. 9, “Integrated Flight Instruction”, p. 9-11
notes.evidence: the flight instructor needs to impress on the learners and ascertain they understand that the introduction to the use of flight instruments does not prepare them for operations in marginal weather or instrument meteorological conditions (IMC).

notes.front: Which early habits does integrated flight instruction establish, and what does it improve on landing?
notes.back: Instrument cross-check, instrument interpretation and aircraft control; landings improve through more precise airspeed control.
notes.explanation: The handbook calls these early habits highly useful to the learner.
notes.source: Aviation Instructor's Handbook (FAA-H-8083-9B), ch. 9, “Development of Habit Patterns”, p. 9-10
notes.evidence: The early establishment of the habits of instrument cross-check, instrument interpretation, and aircraft control is highly useful to the learner. The habitual attention to instrument indications leads to improved landings because of more precise airspeed control.

notes.front: Whose needs does a traditional grading scale such as “excellent, good, fair, poor” often meet, and whose does it not?
notes.back: It often meets the instructor’s needs but not the learner’s.
notes.explanation: The handbook gives “excellent, good, fair, poor” and “exceeds standards, meets standards, needs more training” as examples.
notes.source: Aviation Instructor's Handbook (FAA-H-8083-9B), ch. 9, “Postflight Evaluation”, p. 9-12
notes.evidence: Traditional assessment depends on a grading scale of "excellent, good, fair, poor" or "exceeds standards, meets standards, needs more training" which often meets the instructor’s needs but not the needs of the learner.

notes.front: What are the parts of collaborative assessment after a flight?
notes.back: A learner self-assessment and a detailed assessment by the instructor, then a discussion comparing the two.
notes.explanation: The self-assessment is meant to stimulate growth in the learner’s thinking and, in turn, behaviour.
notes.source: Aviation Instructor's Handbook (FAA-H-8083-9B), ch. 9, “Postflight Evaluation”, p. 9-12
notes.evidence: Collaborative assessment includes learner self-assessment and a detailed assessment by the aviation instructor. The purpose of the self-assessment is to stimulate growth in the learner’s thought processes and, in turn, behaviors. The self-assessment is followed by an in-depth discussion between the instructor and the learner

notes.front: When should the flight instructor debrief a learner after a solo flight?
notes.back: Immediately after the flight.
notes.explanation: With the flight vividly etched in the learner’s memory, questions come quickly.
notes.source: Aviation Instructor's Handbook (FAA-H-8083-9B), ch. 9, “Post-Solo Debriefing”, p. 9-12
notes.evidence: It is very important for the flight instructor to debrief a learner immediately after a solo flight. With the flight vividly etched in the learner’s memory, questions about the flight will come quickly.

notes.front: Does correcting learner errors mean taking over as soon as a mistake is made?
notes.back: No: safety permitting, it is frequently better to let learners go part of the way into the mistake and find a way out.
notes.explanation: Safety is the condition for letting the mistake develop.
notes.source: Aviation Instructor's Handbook (FAA-H-8083-9B), ch. 9, “Correction of Learner Errors”, p. 9-12
notes.evidence: Correction of learner errors does not include the practice of taking over from learners immediately when a mistake is made. Safety permitting, it is frequently better to let learners progress part of the way into the mistake and find a way out.

notes.front: What does the handbook call by far the most important flight instructor responsibility?
notes.back: Providing guidance and restraint with respect to learners’ solo operations.
notes.explanation: The flight instructor is the only person in a position to decide a learner is ready for solo operations.
notes.source: Aviation Instructor's Handbook (FAA-H-8083-9B), ch. 9, “Pilot Supervision”, p. 9-13
notes.evidence: Flight instructors have the responsibility to provide guidance and restraint with respect to the solo operations of their learners. This is by far the most important flight instructor responsibility. The flight instructor is the only person in a position to make the determination a learner is ready for solo operations.

notes.front: For how long is the instructor’s signature on FAA Form 8710-1 valid, and how does it relate to the logbook endorsement?
notes.back: 60 days; the flight proficiency endorsement in the logbook is the same, and the two dates should match.
notes.explanation: The 60 days is the handbook's figure. The regulation, §61.39(a)(6)(i), and AC 61-65K instead require training logged within the 2 calendar months before the month of application.
notes.source: Aviation Instructor's Handbook (FAA-H-8083-9B), ch. 9, “Practical Test Recommendations”, p. 9-13
notes.evidence: When the instructor endorses the applicant for the practical test, his or her signature on the FAA Form 8710-1, Airman Certificate and/or Rating Application, is valid for 60 days. This is also true with the flight proficiency endorsement that is placed in the applicant’s logbook or training record (Advisory Circular (AC) 61-65). These two dates should be the same.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-26 · FAA-S-ACS-25 and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: A learner has made almost no mistakes in five lessons and now shrugs off the instructor’s corrections as unimportant. What does the handbook advise?
notes.back: B) Raise the standard of performance for each lesson, demanding greater effort
notes.explanation: Fast learners may assume correcting errors is unimportant, and the overconfidence that follows leads to faulty performance.
notes.source: Aviation Instructor's Handbook (FAA-H-8083-9B), ch. 8, “Providing Adequate Instruction”, p. 8-2
notes.evidence: Because these learners make few mistakes, they may assume that the correction of errors is unimportant. Overconfidence may result, which leads to faulty performance. For these learners, the instructor constantly raises the standard of performance for each lesson, demanding greater effort.
notes.choices:
A) Invent a few deficiencies so he stays humble
B) Raise the standard of performance for each lesson, demanding greater effort
C) Ease off, since he is clearly ahead
D) Assign more easily attained goals
notes.choicesExplained: A: the handbook says deficiencies should not be invented; unfair criticism destroys confidence in the instructor. C: easing off does nothing about the overconfidence it warns of. D: easier goals are its remedy for learners held back by discouragement or lack of confidence.

notes.front: On Monday an instructor lets a learner’s 150-foot altitude excursions pass without comment. On Wednesday she sharply criticises the same excursions. Which rule for minimising frustration is she breaking?
notes.back: C) Be consistent
notes.explanation: The same thing is acceptable one day and not the next, which confuses the learner.
notes.source: Aviation Instructor's Handbook (FAA-H-8083-9B), ch. 8, “Minimizing Learner Frustration”, p. 8-4
notes.evidence: If the same thing is acceptable one day and unacceptable the next, the learner becomes confused. The instructor’s philosophy and actions need to be consistent.
notes.choices:
A) Motivate learners
B) Give credit when due
C) Be consistent
D) Admit errors
notes.choicesExplained: A: motivation is about learners seeing the purpose of a lesson. B: credit is about noticing work done well. D: admitting errors is about the instructor’s own mistakes.

notes.front: Mid-lesson, a learner points out that the instructor quoted the wrong traffic pattern altitude for the airport. The instructor is embarrassed. What does the handbook suggest?
notes.back: A) Honestly acknowledge the mistake
notes.explanation: Honest acknowledgement wins respect, while covering up or bluffing is quickly sensed and destroys confidence.
notes.source: Aviation Instructor's Handbook (FAA-H-8083-9B), ch. 8, “Minimizing Learner Frustration”, p. 8-4
notes.evidence: The instructor can win the respect of learners by honestly acknowledging mistakes. If the instructor tries to cover up or bluff, learners sense it quickly. Such behavior tends to destroy learner confidence in the instructor.
notes.choices:
A) Honestly acknowledge the mistake
B) Bluff and move on quickly
C) Turn the talk to the learner’s own errors
D) Say both figures are acceptable
notes.choicesExplained: B and D: both are the cover-up or bluff that learners sense quickly. C: deflecting does not admit the error either, and does nothing for the learner’s confidence.

notes.front: A learner whose personal minimums call for a 2,000-foot ceiling wants to go “just this once” under a legal 1,200-foot ceiling. Which item of the instructor’s code of ethics best fits the instructor’s reply?
notes.back: D) Adhere to prudent operating practices and personal operating parameters
notes.explanation: The flight is legal, so the law is not the issue; the code separately asks for adherence to prudent practices and personal operating parameters.
notes.source: Aviation Instructor's Handbook (FAA-H-8083-9B), ch. 5, “Instructor's Code of Ethics”, p. 5-3
notes.evidence: 6. Adhere to prudent operating practices and personal operating parameters, and 7. Adhere to applicable laws and regulations.
notes.choices:
A) Act with responsibility and courtesy
B) Be accountable for his or her actions
C) Adhere to applicable laws and regulations
D) Adhere to prudent operating practices and personal operating parameters
notes.choicesExplained: A: courtesy and responsibility are not what is at stake. C: the flight would be legal, so this item does not stop it. B: accountability is about owning actions afterwards, not the limit being broken.

notes.front: A flight school manager proposes failing any stage check in which a learner does not follow every recommended practice in the Aviator’s Model Code of Conduct. What does the handbook say about the code that bears on this?
notes.back: D) It is not a “standard” and is not intended to be implemented as one
notes.explanation: The code offers principles that complement and supplement what is merely legal; it is guidance, not a pass mark.
notes.source: Aviation Instructor's Handbook (FAA-H-8083-9B), ch. 8, “Aviator's Model Code of Conduct”, p. 8-6
notes.evidence: Its principles both complement and supplement what is merely legal. The Code of Conduct is not a "standard" and is not intended to be implemented as such.
notes.choices:
A) It is a regulation in part 61
B) It applies only to airline crews
C) It replaces the Airman Certification Standards
D) It is not a “standard” and is not intended to be implemented as one
notes.choicesExplained: A: the handbook presents it as guidance, not regulation. B: it is written for general aviation pilots. C: nothing in the handbook links it to replacing the certification standards.

notes.front: An instructor lectures learners on the importance of checklists but runs his own preflight from memory in front of them. What does the handbook suggest?
notes.back: A) Learners tend to imitate him, so he should emphasise safety by example
notes.explanation: Learners treat the instructor as a role model, and advocacy means little if he does not practise it consistently.
notes.source: Aviation Instructor's Handbook (FAA-H-8083-9B), ch. 8, “Safety Practices and Accident Prevention”, p. 8-6
notes.evidence: Generally, learners consider their instructor to be a role model whose habits they attempt to imitate, whether consciously or unconsciously. The instructor’s advocacy and description of safety practices mean little to a learner if the instructor does not demonstrate them consistently.
notes.choices:
A) Learners tend to imitate him, so he should emphasise safety by example
B) More lectures will fix it
C) Learners will ignore both the lecture and his example
D) Learners will follow the lecture, so nothing needs to change
notes.choicesExplained: D and B: the handbook says advocacy and description mean little without consistent demonstration. C: the handbook says learners tend to imitate their instructor’s habits, not ignore them.

notes.front: An instructor gives one direction and then its opposite, snaps at a learner for an error he laughed off last week, and jokes flippantly through a stall recovery. Which professional quality is most at fault?
notes.back: D) Demeanor
notes.explanation: Contradictory directions, reacting differently to the same error, and flippancy are exactly what the handbook says a successful instructor avoids.
notes.source: Aviation Instructor's Handbook (FAA-H-8083-9B), ch. 8, “Demeanor”, p. 8-9
notes.evidence: The successful instructor avoids contradictory directions, reacting differently to similar or identical errors at different times, demanding unreasonable performance or progress, criticizing a learner unfairly, or presenting an overbearing manner or air of flippancy.
notes.choices:
A) Acceptance of the learner
B) Personal appearance
C) Proper language
D) Demeanor
notes.choicesExplained: B: nothing is said about dress or cleanliness. C: there is no profanity. A: he is not rejecting the learner as a person; his manner is the problem.

notes.front: During a lesson the instructor notices several small errors and plans to remember them all for the debrief. What does the handbook recommend?
notes.back: C) Keep written notes so the critique covers every area noticed
notes.explanation: Written notes help the instructor cover all the areas noticed during the flight.
notes.source: Aviation Instructor's Handbook (FAA-H-8083-9B), ch. 8, “Keeping the Learner Informed”, p. 8-10
notes.evidence: These critiques should be in a written format, such as notes, to aid the instructor in covering all areas that were noticed during the flight or lesson.
notes.choices:
A) Save them for the next stage check
B) Mention only the largest error
C) Keep written notes so the critique covers every area noticed
D) Skip the critique if the flight was safe
notes.choicesExplained: A: the learner should be kept informed as manoeuvres are completed or at the postflight critique. B: the notes are meant to cover all areas noticed. D: keeping the learner informed does not depend on nothing going wrong.

notes.front: The instructor flies a steep turn while the learner talks her through it: clear the area, roll in, add back pressure, lead the roll-out. Which step of the telling-and-doing technique is this?
notes.back: D) Learner tells, instructor does
notes.explanation: The learner plays the instructor, saying what to do and how, while the instructor flies.
notes.source: Aviation Instructor's Handbook (FAA-H-8083-9B), ch. 9, “Learner Tells—Instructor Does”, p. 9-8
notes.evidence: Second, the learner tells as the instructor does. In this step, the learner actually plays the role of instructor, telling the instructor what to do and how to do it.
notes.choices:
A) Instructor tells, instructor does
B) Learner tells, learner does
C) Instructor evaluates while the learner performs
D) Learner tells, instructor does
notes.choicesExplained: A: here the learner is passive. B: here the learner would be flying. C: here too the learner would be flying.

notes.front: Handing control back, the learner says, “You have the flight controls.” The instructor has not yet replied. What should the learner do?
notes.back: D) Keep flying until the instructor says, “I have the flight controls”
notes.explanation: The learner follows the same procedure the instructor used, and control passes only with the acknowledgement.
notes.source: Aviation Instructor's Handbook (FAA-H-8083-9B), ch. 9, “Positive Exchange of Flight Controls”, p. 9-9
notes.evidence: When returning the controls to the instructor, the learner should follow the same procedure the instructor used when giving control to the learner. The learner should stay on the controls and keep flying the aircraft until the instructor says, "I have the flight controls."
notes.choices:
A) Let go at once, since the words have been said
B) Let go once the instructor’s hand touches the yoke
C) Glance across, then release the controls
D) Keep flying until the instructor says, “I have the flight controls”
notes.choicesExplained: A, B and C: each lets go without the spoken acknowledgement, leaving doubt about who is flying.

notes.front: While the learner practises slow flight, the instructor asks her to find the heading to a nearby airport on the chart. What is the instructor doing?
notes.back: C) Teaching her to divide attention between the distracting task and controlling the aircraft
notes.explanation: Determining a heading on a chart is one of the handbook’s own examples of distractions for this training.
notes.source: Aviation Instructor's Handbook (FAA-H-8083-9B), ch. 9, “Use of Distractions”, p. 9-10
notes.evidence: Instructor responsibilities include teaching the learner to divide his or her attention between the distracting task and maintaining control of the aircraft. The following are examples of distractions that can be used for this training: ⦁ Drop a pencil. Ask the learner to pick it up. ⦁ Ask the learner to determine a heading to an airport using a chart.
notes.choices:
A) Filling time in the practice area
B) Checking her chart reading for the knowledge test
C) Teaching her to divide attention between the distracting task and controlling the aircraft
D) Setting her up to fail so the lesson is repeated
notes.choicesExplained: B: the chart task is only the distraction; the point is keeping control. A and D: the handbook presents distractions as deliberate training, not filler or a trap.

notes.front: An instructor plans to teach climbs and descents by outside references only, leaving the instruments until the learner starts an instrument rating. How does this fit integrated flight instruction?
notes.back: C) It does not: instrument references should begin the first time each new manoeuvre is introduced
notes.explanation: For integrated instruction to be fully effective, instrument references start with each manoeuvre’s first introduction.
notes.source: Aviation Instructor's Handbook (FAA-H-8083-9B), ch. 9, “Integrated Flight Instruction”, p. 9-10
notes.evidence: For this type of instruction to be fully effective, the use of instrument references should begin the first time each new maneuver is introduced.
notes.choices:
A) It fits: instruments come after the private pilot certificate
B) It fits, provided the controls are handled differently on instruments
C) It does not: instrument references should begin the first time each new manoeuvre is introduced
D) It does not: outside references should wait until the instruments are mastered
notes.choicesExplained: A: delaying instruments is what integrated instruction avoids. B: no distinction in handling the controls is permitted. D: outside and instrument references are taught together, not one after the other.

notes.front: During a lesson the instructor sees that a learner’s forward slips have fallen below standard and decides the task needs reteaching. What sequence does the handbook give?
notes.back: B) Demonstrate it, let the learner practise under direction, then evaluate by observing the performance
notes.explanation: The instructor reteaches by demonstrating, directing practice, then observing.
notes.source: Aviation Instructor's Handbook (FAA-H-8083-9B), ch. 9, “Assessment of Piloting Ability”, p. 9-11
notes.evidence: If the instructor observes a deficiency and determines a task needs reteaching, the instructor demonstrates the maneuver, allows the learner to practice the maneuver under direction, and finally evaluates learner accomplishment by observing the performance.
notes.choices:
A) Record an unsatisfactory grade and move on
B) Demonstrate it, let the learner practise under direction, then evaluate by observing the performance
C) Assign reading and retest next week
D) Have the learner self-assess only
notes.choicesExplained: A and C: neither reteaches the task in the aircraft. D: self-assessment alone leaves out the demonstration and directed practice.

notes.front: An instructor is supervising a first solo with a handheld radio. Which of these fits the handbook’s guidance?
notes.back: D) Keep calls to a minimum, use the radio to end the solo if a problem develops, and stay silent on short final
notes.explanation: The radio lets the instructor terminate the solo if a situation develops, but talk is kept to a minimum.
notes.source: Aviation Instructor's Handbook (FAA-H-8083-9B), ch. 9, “First Solo Flight”, p. 9-12
notes.evidence: A radio enables the instructor to terminate the solo operation if he or she observes a situation developing. The flight instructor needs should use good judgment when communicating with a solo learner. Keep all radio communications to a minimum. Do not talk to the learner on short final of the landing approach.
notes.choices:
A) Coach the learner round every leg of the pattern
B) Talk the learner down on short final
C) Leave the radio behind so the learner feels independent
D) Keep calls to a minimum, use the radio to end the solo if a problem develops, and stay silent on short final
notes.choicesExplained: A: communications should be kept to a minimum. B: the handbook says not to talk to the learner on short final. C: the handbook wants the instructor to have a radio if possible.

notes.front: A learner flies a flawless rectangular course, but the instructor suspects she has memorised it without grasping the principles. What does the handbook suggest?
notes.back: B) Have her vary it slightly, combine it with other operations, or apply its elements to other manoeuvres
notes.explanation: Learners who do not understand the principles will probably not manage the variation.
notes.source: Aviation Instructor's Handbook (FAA-H-8083-9B), ch. 9, “Correction of Learner Errors”, p. 9-12
notes.evidence: When the instructor suspects this, learners should be required to vary the performance of the maneuver slightly, combine it with other operations, or apply the same elements to the performance of other maneuvers. Learners who do not understand the principles involved will probably not be able to do this successfully.
notes.choices:
A) Sign it off, since correct performance proves understanding
B) Have her vary it slightly, combine it with other operations, or apply its elements to other manoeuvres
C) Take the controls and demonstrate it again
D) Move straight on to the next manoeuvre
notes.choicesExplained: A: the handbook says learners may perform correctly without fully understanding. C: a demonstration does not test her understanding. D: moving on leaves the suspicion untested.

notes.front: An applicant is strong in most areas. The instructor wants to sign the recommendation without checking the emergency tasks, because “the examiner rarely asks those”. What does the handbook expect?
notes.back: A) A thorough demonstration, never less than the complete procedure in the applicable standards
notes.explanation: The demonstration must show the knowledge and skill level the certificate or rating requires.
notes.source: Aviation Instructor's Handbook (FAA-H-8083-9B), ch. 9, “Practical Test Recommendations”, p. 9-13
notes.evidence: A flight instructor who makes a practical test recommendation for an applicant seeking a certificate or rating should require the applicant to thoroughly demonstrate the knowledge and skill level required for that certificate or rating. This demonstration should in no instance be less than the complete procedure prescribed in the applicable ACS/PTS.
notes.choices:
A) A thorough demonstration, never less than the complete procedure in the applicable standards
B) Check only the tasks examiners usually test
C) Sign now and review the weak tasks after the test
D) Leave it to the examiner to judge readiness
notes.choicesExplained: B: the demonstration should never be less than the complete procedure. C: the demonstration comes before the recommendation. D: examiners rely on the instructor’s recommendation as evidence of qualification.

notes.front: A learner’s steep turns sit right at the edge of the practical test tolerances, and he sees no reason to improve. What should the instructor help him understand?
notes.back: A) Meeting the standard provides only a limited margin of safety
notes.explanation: Instructors are to explain why pilots are trained to standards and how those standards are set.
notes.source: Aviation Instructor's Handbook (FAA-H-8083-9B), ch. 8, “Flight Instructor Responsibilities”, p. 8-5
notes.evidence: It is also important to provide an understanding of why pilots are trained to standards, how these standards are set, and that meeting the standard provides a limited margin of safety.
notes.choices:
A) Meeting the standard provides only a limited margin of safety
B) Standards matter only on the day of the practical test
C) Meeting the standard guarantees a safe flight
D) Tolerances are relaxed after certification
notes.choicesExplained: C: the handbook says the opposite: the margin is limited. B and D: nothing in the handbook supports treating the standards as a one-day hurdle.

notes.front: What is the main difference between the telling-and-doing technique and the demonstration-performance method?
notes.back: The transition “learner tells, instructor does”, between the second and third steps.
notes.explanation: The handbook’s comparison figure shows the similarities as well as this difference.
notes.source: Aviation Instructor's Handbook (FAA-H-8083-9B), ch. 9, “Instructor Tells—Instructor Does”, p. 9-7
notes.evidence: This comparison of steps in the teaching process, the demonstration-performance method, and the telling-and-doing technique highlights similarities as well as differences. The main difference in the telling-and-doing technique is the important transition, learner tells—instructor does, which occurs between the second and third step.

notes.front: The telling-and-doing technique and the positive exchange of flight controls both have three steps. What does each set of three steps govern?
notes.back: Telling-and-doing: who explains and who flies while a manoeuvre is taught. Positive exchange: the spoken handover of control between pilots.
notes.explanation: The exchange steps are the words “You have the flight controls”, “I have the flight controls” and “You have the flight controls” again.
notes.source: Flight Instructor for Airplane Category ACS (FAA-S-ACS-25), Appendix, “Positive Exchange of Flight Controls”, p. 107
notes.evidence: The FAA recommends a positive three-step process for exchanging flight controls between pilots: • When one pilot seeks to have the other pilot take control of the aircraft, they will say, "You have the flight controls."
